podcast.title: First Show October 17, 1975 – Pre-dates Sex Pistols and The Clash; 1980 Ontario Place Riot
podcast.body: Teenage Head formed in Hamilton, Ontario, and played their first show on October 17, 1975 at Westdale High School — three weeks before the Sex Pistols played their first gig, and nine months before The Clash formed. They were a major force in Canadian punk, combining elements of the Ramones, New York Dolls, and 1950s rock and roll. Their profile peaked with a 1980 show at Ontario Place in Toronto where thousands tried to get in; what followed became an infamous riot. American radio programmers loved the music but balked at the band name (for obvious reasons), prompting a temporary rename to "Teenage Heads" for US purposes. Just before a crucial US showcase in September 1980, guitarist Gord Lewis was in a serious car accident, canceling the shows and closing the window of opportunity. Original singer Frankie Venom died of throat cancer in 2008; the band continues with Dave Rave on vocals more than 40 years later. "Long after most of their original punk rock contemporaries called it quits, or died off, Teenage Head still with us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canadian Band Longevity and Singer's Death
podcast.body: Teenage Head had been active since 1975 before their singer, Frankie Venom, died "last year" (relative to the interview), marking them as another enduring Canadian band with a significant history. "Teenage head had been around since 1975 before singer Frankie Venom died last year."

podcast.title: Cancon Boosted Success (1970s)
podcast.body: Teenage Head was among the Canadian rock bands that experienced a boost in their careers due to the Cancon rules introduced in the 1970s. "Just on the rock side, we had Rush, April Wine, the Guess Who, Triumph, Crobar, Teenage Head, Max Webster, Chilowac, FM, Saga, and a foot-and-cold water."

podcast.title: Early Support for Headstones
podcast.body: Gord Lewis was a vocal and enthusiastic supporter of the Headstones, providing confidence to the younger band and affirming their talent during their formative years. "We sat in our hotel room with Gord. Oh, that was like one of those crazy moments because I grew up idolizing Teenage Hits."

podcast.title: Gord Lewis's Murder
podcast.body: Gord Lewis, the guitarist and founding member of Teenage Head, was tragically murdered, with his body discovered in his Hamilton apartment on August 7th. "Gord Lewis, guitarist and founding member of Teenage Head. This is so sad. His body was found in his Hamilton apartment on August 7th."

podcast.title: Idolization and Influence
podcast.body: Hugh Dillon grew up idolizing Teenage Head, buying their records and learning to play guitar from their music, making them a significant influence on his early career. "I grew up idolizing Teenage Hits. One of the first records I bought, that was a rock record."

podcast.title: International Recognition Gap
podcast.body: Despite influencing numerous bands across Canada, both sides of the American border, and even in the UK, Teenage Head never achieved the international attention they were considered to deserve. "Teenage Head never received the international attention they deserved. Although they influence many many bands across Canada on both sides of the American border and even in the UK."

podcast.title: Potential Delay in Discovery of Death
podcast.body: It is believed that Gord Lewis may have been deceased for a couple of days before his body was found, during which time his son Jonathan reportedly posted desperate messages online. "We do know that Gord may have been dead for a couple of days while Jonathan posted desperate messages online."

xref.title: Possible First All-Female Canadian Punk Band; Shoeshine Boy Written About Emanuel Jaques Murder (1977)
xref.body: The Curse are contenders with the B-Girls for the title of Canada's first all-female punk band, having been ready to perform as early as May 1977. The following month they played CBGB in New York on a bill with the Viletones, Diodes, and Teenage Head. They were more intense than the B-Girls — member Mickey Skin performed with a fake lobotomy scar and the band had an explicitly feminist agenda, often starting food fights at shows. Their most controversial song, "Shoeshine Boy," was written about the 1977 murder of 12-year-old Emanuel Jaques in Toronto: a boy shining shoes on Yonge Street who was offered $35 to help move photographic equipment, then tortured and raped for 12 hours before being strangled and drowned in a kitchen sink. The crime catalyzed the city's cleanup of its red-light district. "They were intent on destroying the patriarchy of music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Hamilton Punk Provocateurs – "Surfin' on Heroin," Nazi Allegations, Cassette "Burn the Flag" (1978)
xref.body: The Forgotten Rebels formed in Hamilton in 1977, about 18 months after Teenage Head. Led by Mickey DeSadist, they were sarcastic, sometimes profane, and featured songs like "Surfin' on Heroin," "Bomb the Boats and Feed the Fish" (about Vietnamese refugees), "No Beatles Reunion," and a song called "Reich 'n' Roll" that drew allegations of anti-Semitism and homophobia; the band maintained it was all satire. Their first release was a six-song cassette called *Burn the Flag* in 1978, followed by *Tomorrow Belongs to Us*. They occasionally attracted crowds of several thousand. "They had a large cult following, although they were never really embraced to the level of Teenage Head."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Friends with Blondie and Ramones; Almost Signed to IRS; Influenced B-52s; Background Vocals on Blondie's Autoamerican
xref.body: The B-Girls formed in Toronto in 1977 with a sound closer to British Invasion mid-1960s than hard punk, though their look and attitude were fully punk. They toured with and opened for Teenage Head, the Viletones, and eventually The Clash, then relocated to New York where they became close with Blondie, the Ramones, the Cramps, and the Dead Boys. Members sang background vocals on Blondie's *Autoamerican* (1980), had demos produced by Debbie Harry and Mick Jones of The Clash, and nearly signed with IRS Records — which chose a Los Angeles band called the Go-Go's instead. The Go-Go's were fans of the B-Girls. The B-Girls' existence and sound also influenced a band from Georgia called the B-52s. No album was released before the original lineup fell apart by 1981. "This Canadian punk band influenced not just Blondie and the Go-Go's, but a band visiting New York from Georgia called the B-52s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Gord Lewis's Early Support
xref.body: Gord Lewis of Teenage Head was a significant fan and supporter of the Headstones, boosting their confidence and believing in their potential. Hugh Dillon recalled a memorable moment sitting in a hotel room with Gord. "Gord Lewis was always such a huge fan that gave us confidence because he was like, you guys can do it."
